messages.text:
We propose the following terms for the three-depot trial.

1. Each party may use trial measurements to operate, maintain and evaluate the sensors. Access to raw failure traces and firmware parameters is limited to named trial-team members who need them for that work. Other maintenance staff may receive fault summaries and recommended actions.
2. Either party may prepare an external report. The author will give the other party 10 working days from receipt of the draft to identify specific passages that reveal restricted data or could identify a route or depot, and explain the concern. Once that period ends, the author may release the report after removing or revising any disputed passages. Silence permits release, subject to the access limits above.
3. The sensor maker may publish aggregate uptime across all three depots under that review process, without separate approval. The figure will omit route and depot identifiers and use a reporting period broad enough to prevent readers from inferring an individual depot’s or route’s result.
4. Either party may immediately share the minimum information needed with people able to address an urgent safety risk. The disclosing party will notify the other as soon as practicable afterward, identifying what was shared, with whom and why.

What maintenance decisions will the external contractor make, and would a fault summary with timestamps, affected equipment and recommended actions let it make those decisions? If a specific task requires a raw trace, we propose naming the responsible technician on the trial team under equivalent confidentiality obligations and limiting access to the trace needed for that task.

We can work from your draft, with the changes below.

Maintenance. The contractor decides whether a unit is safe to leave in service, what to replace or recalibrate, and whether the fault is sensor, mounting, power, or communications. A fault summary with affected equipment, a time window no finer than the shift, and recommended actions is enough for routine work. It is not enough when the summary and the observed fault disagree, or when a replacement fails the post-repair check. In those cases, name the technician on the trial team, bind them to the same confidentiality terms, and release only the trace for that unit and that fault. Do not include employee identifiers in the trace package.

Identification. Exact depot-and-time pairs can identify staff. External text, including aggregates and fault examples, must not pair a depot or route with a timestamp finer than a calendar month. Internal repair packages may use the precision the job needs and stay inside the named team.

Reporting we need.
- Monthly aggregates for our board: uptime, fault counts, and false-alert rate, pooled across all three depots, month-level only, no route or depot split. We may circulate that internally without your approval. External use of the same figures follows the review in section 2.
- Your all-depot uptime figure is acceptable on the same basis: no depot or route identifier, period no shorter than one month, and the section 2 review.

Review. Ten working days is acceptable for routine external reports. Silence allows release only after the author has removed every passage the other party timely flagged as restricted or identifying. A flag must name the passage and the concern. Unflagged text may go out. Disputed text stays out until revised or dropped; it is not released over an unresolved objection.

Urgent safety. This cannot depend on prior clearance. Either party may immediately give authorities, and others who can reduce the risk, the minimum needed for a serious incident or an imminent safety risk. Notice to the other party follows as soon as practicable, stating what was shared, with whom, and why. That after-the-fact notice is not a request for approval, and neither party will promise regulators prior clearance.

If that allocation — routine summaries, named-technician traces, month-level aggregates, objection-based hold on disputed passages only, and unblocked authority notice — is acceptable, we can treat it as the operating text.
We accept your changes. Our draft, as amended by your message, is the agreed operating text for the three-depot trial.

We need three amendments to the operating text. The pooled monthly figures and the urgent-authority rule stay as agreed.

Small cells. Two depots can support a separate internal count. One cannot: its volume is low enough that a depot figure would function as a vehicle or staff identifier. Ordinary circulation, internal or external, stays pooled across all three depots, month-level, with no depot or route split. Any cell in which one vehicle accounts for the observations, or which pairs a depot or route with a time finer than a calendar month, is suppressed. We will not publish a depot league table to “complete” the set.

Confidential inspection. If a documented threshold is crossed, a board subcommittee of three — the safety lead and two named board members — may inspect the suppressed depot result. Thresholds: a serious incident or imminent safety risk at that depot; a sensor-related removal from service; or a month in which that depot’s serious-fault count is at least twice the pooled rate and at least three events. Inspection is read-only, on a need basis, within two working days of the safety lead recording that a threshold was met. No copies outside that subcommittee, no contractor, no external report. A one-line log records date, threshold, and who inspected. This is not a publication path and does not require your prior clearance.

Incident traces. Routine repair stays on the agreed summary, with a named-technician trace only when the summary and the fault disagree or a post-repair check fails. A different clock applies when a unit is pulled for a serious incident, a near-miss, or a safety hold. The safety lead or the depot maintenance supervisor may authorize one named contractor technician, already bound to the trial confidentiality terms, to receive the trace for that unit and that incident window only, with no employee identifiers. Target release is within four hours of the request during staffed hours, and before the next shift otherwise. That release does not wait on the ten-day review. We notify you as soon as practicable afterward — what was released, to whom, and which trigger — and that notice is not a request for approval.

If the subcommittee list, the twice-pooled-and-three-event threshold, or the four-hour trace clock is too wide, say what you would narrow. We need those three points decided before sign-off.

We accept the three-person subcommittee and the proposed trace-release clock. We also accept the twice-pooled threshold with a three-event minimum, provided both teams compare rates using the same denominator. We propose the following addendum.

1. **Ordinary reporting.** The board may receive monthly uptime, fault counts and false-alert rates pooled across all three depots. Ordinary internal and external reports omit depot and route splits, suppress any cell based on one vehicle, and omit breakdowns from which a suppressed result could be calculated by subtraction. The sensor maker may publish pooled uptime for periods of at least one month under the agreed ten-working-day external review.

2. **Confidential board inspection.** Within two working days after the safety lead records a qualifying event, the safety lead and two board members named in advance may inspect the affected depot’s suppressed result on a need-to-know basis, without prior clearance. A serious incident, an imminent safety risk or a sensor-related removal from service each qualifies on its own. For the monthly trigger, we propose using **serious faults per 1,000 monitored vehicle-hours**. The depot must record at least three serious faults that month, and its rate must reach at least twice the all-depot rate for the same month. The pooled rate uses total faults divided by total monitored vehicle-hours across all three depots.

   The read-only view may show the relevant result and a brief account of the failure, its operational consequence and the corrective action. It omits employee and vehicle identifiers, raw traces and firmware parameters. A single-vehicle result can still identify its operator, so access ends with the three named reviewers. They may report the corrective action to the full board only in a form that protects the operator and the suppressed result. Inspection permits no copies, contractor access or external reporting. The log records the inspection date, trigger and reviewers.

3. **Incident trace access.** Routine repairs follow the agreed summary and named-technician rules. When a unit is pulled for a serious incident, near-miss or safety hold, the safety lead or depot maintenance supervisor may authorize one named contractor technician bound by the trial confidentiality terms to join the trial team for that incident. Release is limited to that unit’s trace for the incident window, with employee identifiers removed and firmware parameters excluded. The target is within four hours of a request during staffed hours and before the next shift for a request outside staffed hours. Release proceeds without prior clearance or external-report review. The transit team will notify the sensor maker as soon as practicable afterward of what was released, to whom and under which trigger.

The agreed urgent-safety rule continues to apply immediately at every tier. Can your team confirm that monitored vehicle-hours are available consistently at all three depots so both teams can apply the monthly trigger as written?

We cannot confirm that monitored vehicle-hours are recorded the same way at all three depots. Treat them as hours a vehicle was in service with the trial sensor powered and reporting, taken from each depot’s existing dispatch or AVL log. Both teams must use that definition and the same month. If a depot cannot produce it for a month, the rate trigger does not fire there that month. Event triggers still do.

We accept the rest of the addendum with one change to section 2. A routine or sensor-related removal from service does not by itself open the depot-level inspection. That view is limited to a serious incident, an imminent safety risk, or the monthly rate test: at least three serious faults, and a rate of serious faults per 1,000 monitored vehicle-hours at least twice the all-depot rate for that month, pooled as total faults divided by total monitored vehicle-hours. The two-working-day, three-reviewer, read-only terms otherwise stand, including no copies, no contractor access, no external reporting, and no employee or vehicle identifiers.

Section 1 and the incident-trace rule are acceptable as written, including the four-hour or next-shift target, identifiers removed, firmware excluded, and after-the-fact notice. Urgent notice to authorities remains immediate and does not wait for clearance or for this inspection.

If you accept the vehicle-hour definition, the missing-denominator fallback, and removal from service not being an independent inspection trigger, this addendum is agreed.

We accept the vehicle-hour definition, the missing-denominator fallback and the revised inspection triggers. The addendum is agreed.

Both teams will count hours when a vehicle was in service with its trial sensor powered and reporting, using each depot’s dispatch or AVL log for the same calendar month. If any depot lacks that denominator, the all-three-depot rate cannot be calculated, so the monthly rate test is unavailable for that month. A serious incident or imminent safety risk still independently opens confidential inspection. Removal from service alone does not.
